title: Recursive Functions — Time & Space Complexity Analysis
subtitle: 66 questions: each shows a concrete recursive function and asks for its complexity. Explanations derive the recurrence step by step.

questions.explanation: Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1). Each call reduces n by 1 and does constant work. The chain has n+1 calls total (n down to 0), so T(n) = O(n). It is NOT O(n^2) because no nested loop or branching occurs — each level does O(1) work.

Each recursive call divides n by 10. The number of digits in n is floor(log10(n)) + 1 = O(log n). Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/10) + O(1), which by the Master Theorem (case 2 with a=1, b=10, f(n)=O(1)) gives T(n) = O(log n).
Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1). Each call processes one element and makes one recursive call with n-1. The recursion goes from n down to 0: n calls total, each O(1). Total time = O(n).

Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1). The exponent decreases by 1 per call, making n recursive calls. This naive power is O(n). Compare with fast exponentiation (halving n each time), which is O(log n) — this version does not halve.

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of this function?

def countdown(n):
    if n <= 0:
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)
    countdown(n - 1)
questions.explanation: Recurrence: T(n) = 2*T(n-1) + O(1). Each call spawns two calls with n-1. The recursion tree has depth n and each level doubles: 1, 2, 4, ..., 2^n nodes. Total calls = 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^n = 2^(n+1) - 1 = O(2^n).
Worst case: target is not in the array. Each call increments i by 1 and does O(1) work. After n calls (i from 0 to n), the base case triggers. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) → T(n) = O(n).
Each call swaps one pair and moves i up and j down. The recursion terminates when i >= j, after n/2 swaps. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-2) + O(1). Unrolling: n/2 calls each doing O(1) = O(n/2) = O(n).
Best case: first characters differ — O(1). Worst case: the string is a palindrome, requiring n/2 comparisons. Each call does O(1) and recurses with a problem of size n-2. T(n) = T(n-2) + O(1) → O(n).

Euclidean GCD: b decreases by at least half every two steps (Fibonacci worst case). By Lamé's theorem, the number of steps is at most 5 times the number of digits in min(a,b), giving O(log(min(a,b))). It is NOT O(min(a,b)) — that would be the subtraction-based algorithm.

Identical recurrence to factorial: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1). The chain of calls goes from n down to 1 (n calls total). Total time = O(n). The mathematical result (n*(n+1)/2) is O(n^2) as a value but computing it recursively this way takes O(n) time.

Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1). Each call halves the search space and does O(1) work. By Master Theorem (a=1, b=2, f(n)=1): n^(log_2 1) = n^0 = 1 = f(n), so T(n) = O(log n). After k halvings, n/2^k = 1 → k = log2(n).

Recurrence: T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n). Two recursive calls on halves, plus O(n) merge. Master Theorem: a=2, b=2, f(n)=n. n^(log_2 2)=n^1=n = f(n), so we are in case 2: T(n) = O(n log n). This holds for all cases (best, worst, average).

questions.question:
What is the worst-case time complexity of this quicksort?

def quicksort(arr, lo, hi):
    if lo >= hi:
        return
    p = partition(arr, lo, hi)   # O(n)
    quicksort(arr, lo, p - 1)
    quicksort(arr, p + 1, hi)
questions.explanation: Worst case: pivot is always the minimum or maximum (e.g., sorted input with naive pivot). Partition produces sub-arrays of size 0 and n-1. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) → T(n) = O(n) + O(n-1) + ... + O(1) = O(n^2). Average case (random pivot) is O(n log n).

When n is even: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) — halves the problem. When n is odd: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) — decrements by 1, but the next call will be even and halve. In the worst case, n alternates odd/even, but the problem still halves every two steps. Overall: T(n) = O(log n).

Recurrence: T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(1). Master Theorem: a=2, b=2, f(n)=1. n^(log_2 2)=n > f(n)=1, so case 1: T(n) = O(n). Every element is visited exactly once (each leaf does O(1)), so total work = O(n). The divide step adds no savings over a loop.

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of this function?

def count_inversions(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr, 0
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left, lc = count_inversions(arr[:mid])
    right, rc = count_inversions(arr[mid:])
    merged, sc = merge_count(left, right)   # O(n)
    return merged, lc + rc + sc
questions.explanation: This is merge sort with inversion counting. Recurrence: T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n). Identical to merge sort: Master Theorem case 2 gives T(n) = O(n log n). The merge_count step counts split inversions in O(n) as part of the merge.

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of Karatsuba multiplication applied recursively?

# Splits each n-digit number into two halves
# Makes 3 recursive calls on n/2-digit numbers
# Combining takes O(n)
questions.explanation: Recurrence: T(n) = 3*T(n/2) + O(n). Master Theorem: a=3, b=2, f(n)=n. n^(log_2 3) ≈ n^1.585 > f(n)=n, so case 1: T(n) = O(n^log_2(3)) ≈ O(n^1.585). This beats naive O(n^2) multiplication. The key is using 3 instead of 4 recursive calls.

options: O(log3 n) which equals O(log n)
questions.explanation: Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/3) + O(1). Master Theorem gives T(n) = O(log3 n). However, log3(n) = log2(n)/log2(3) = O(log n). Ternary search has the same asymptotic complexity as binary search, just with a smaller constant. The answer O(log3 n) = O(log n) is the most precise.

Recurrence: T(n) = 3*T(2n/3) + O(1). Master Theorem: a=3, b=3/2, f(n)=1. n^(log_(3/2) 3) = n^(log3/log(3/2)) ≈ n^2.709. Since n^2.709 >> O(1), case 1 applies: T(n) = O(n^(log_(3/2) 3)) ≈ O(n^2.7). Stooge sort is a deliberately inefficient algorithm.

questions.question:
What is the average-case time complexity of quicksort with a random pivot?

# Partition is O(n)
# On average, pivot splits array roughly in half
questions.explanation: With a random pivot, the expected split is roughly n/4 to 3n/4. The expected recurrence is T(n) = T(n/4) + T(3n/4) + O(n). By solving this (or using the fact that the recursion tree has depth O(log n) and O(n) work per level), the average case is O(n log n). Worst case remains O(n^2).

Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1). The recursion tree is a binary tree of depth n. Upper bound: T(n) < 2*T(n-1) → T(n) = O(2^n). More precisely, T(n) = O(phi^n) where phi ≈ 1.618, but O(2^n) is the standard answer. The same subproblems are recomputed exponentially many times.

Every node is visited exactly once (two recursive calls per node, each returning the height of a subtree). Total calls = n. Each call does O(1) work. Recurrence: T(n) = T(L) + T(R) + O(1) where L+R = n-1. Summing over all nodes: O(n). O(h) describes only the recursion depth, not the total work.
Each node is visited exactly once and O(1) work is done per visit. Recurrence: T(n) = T(L) + T(R) + O(1). The recursion visits all n nodes regardless of tree shape (balanced or skewed). Total: O(n).

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of this function?

def sum_tree(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0
    left_sum = sum_tree(root.left)
    right_sum = sum_tree(root.right)
    return root.val + left_sum + right_sum
questions.explanation: Visits every node exactly once, doing O(1) per node. Recurrence: T(n) = T(L) + T(R) + O(1) = O(n). This is identical in structure to count_nodes or tree_height — all simple single-pass tree traversals are O(n).

Recurrence: T(m,n) = T(m-1,n) + T(m,n-1) + O(1). Without memoization, the same subproblems are recomputed. The recursion tree has depth m+n and branches at each node, giving T(m,n) = O(2^(m+n)) in the worst case. With memoization it reduces to O(m*n).

Identical recurrence to naive Fibonacci: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) = O(2^n). Each call branches into two, and overlapping subproblems are recomputed. Without memoization this is exponential. With memoization or DP it becomes O(n).

Recurrence: T(n) = 3*T(n/3) + O(1). Master Theorem: a=3, b=3, f(n)=1. n^(log_3 3) = n^1 = n. Since n >> O(1), case 1: T(n) = O(n^(log_3 3)) = O(n). Despite three recursive calls, each on n/3 data, the total work across all levels is O(n).

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of this function?

def all_subsets(arr, i, current):
    if i == len(arr):
        print(current)
        return
    all_subsets(arr, i + 1, current)            # exclude arr[i]
    all_subsets(arr, i + 1, current + [arr[i]]) # include arr[i]
questions.explanation: Recurrence: T(n) = 2*T(n-1) + O(1), giving O(2^n) recursive calls. But each leaf prints a subset. The average subset has n/2 elements and printing takes O(n/2) time. Total work = O(2^n) calls × O(n) print cost = O(n * 2^n). If printing were O(1), it would be O(2^n).

There are n! permutations. Each is printed in O(n) time. The number of recursive calls is sum(n!/(n-k)!) for k=0..n ≈ e*n! = O(n!). Each leaf prints in O(n). Total: O(n * n!). If printing were O(1), it would be O(n!).

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of the Towers of Hanoi with n disks?

def hanoi(n, source, target, auxiliary):
    if n == 0:
        return
    hanoi(n - 1, source, auxiliary, target)
    print(f'Move disk {n} from {source} to {target}')
    hanoi(n - 1, auxiliary, target, source)
questions.explanation: Recurrence: T(n) = 2*T(n-1) + O(1). Each call makes two sub-calls with n-1. Unrolling: T(n) = 2^n * T(0) + 2^(n-1) + ... + 1 = O(2^n). This is optimal — moving n disks requires exactly 2^n - 1 moves. There is no faster algorithm.

options: O(C(n,k)) which is O(2^n) worst case
questions.explanation: Without memoization, each call branches into two sub-calls. The recursion tree mirrors Pascal's triangle, and the number of calls equals the sum of all C(i,j) for relevant i,j. In the worst case (k ≈ n/2), this is O(2^n). With memoization: O(n*k).

The number of nodes explored is bounded by n * (n-1) * (n-2) * ... = O(n!) (column choices decrease). The is_safe check at depth row costs O(row) ≤ O(n). Total: O(n! * n). O(n^n) overestimates (many branches are pruned by the safety check).

This is structurally identical to naive Fibonacci. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) = O(2^n) without memoization. The same subproblems (count_ways(k) for k < n) are recomputed exponentially many times.

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of this function?

def generate_binary_strings(n, current=''):
    if n == 0:
        print(current)
        return
    generate_binary_strings(n - 1, current + '0')
    generate_binary_strings(n - 1, current + '1')
questions.explanation: Recurrence: T(n) = 2*T(n-1) + O(n). The O(n) comes from string concatenation (current + '0' creates a new string of length n-k). There are 2^n leaves, each printing a string of length n. Total work: O(n * 2^n). If strings were passed by reference with no copy cost, it would be O(2^n) calls.

questions.question: What does the Master Theorem say about T(n) = 4*T(n/2) + n?
questions.explanation: Master Theorem: a=4, b=2, f(n)=n. Compute n^(log_b a) = n^(log_2 4) = n^2. Compare with f(n)=n: n^2 > n, so case 1 applies (f(n) = O(n^(log_b a - eps))). T(n) = O(n^2).

questions.question: What does the Master Theorem say about T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + n^2?
questions.explanation: Master Theorem: a=2, b=2, f(n)=n^2. n^(log_2 2)=n^1=n. Compare: f(n)=n^2 >> n, so case 3 applies (f(n) = Omega(n^(log_b a + eps))). Check regularity: 2*(n/2)^2 = n^2/2 ≤ c*n^2 for c=1/2 < 1. T(n) = O(n^2).

questions.question: What does the Master Theorem say about T(n) = 3*T(n/3) + n?
questions.explanation: Master Theorem: a=3, b=3, f(n)=n. n^(log_3 3)=n^1=n. f(n)=n = Theta(n^(log_b a)) = Theta(n), so case 2: T(n) = O(n^(log_b a) * log n) = O(n log n). This is the same recurrence as merge sort but with 3 equal parts — same result.

questions.question: What does the Master Theorem say about T(n) = T(n/2) + n?
questions.explanation: Master Theorem: a=1, b=2, f(n)=n. n^(log_2 1)=n^0=1. f(n)=n >> 1, so case 3: T(n) = O(f(n)) = O(n). Regularity: 1*(n/2) = n/2 ≤ c*n for c=1/2. T(n) = O(n). The dominant cost is the first level (n work), with subsequent levels halving: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = 2n = O(n).

questions.question: What does the Master Theorem say about T(n) = 8*T(n/2) + n^2?
questions.explanation: Master Theorem: a=8, b=2, f(n)=n^2. n^(log_2 8)=n^3. Compare: n^3 >> n^2, so case 1: T(n) = O(n^3). This is the recurrence for naive matrix multiplication (Strassen reduces it to T(n) = 7*T(n/2) + O(n^2), giving O(n^2.807)).

questions.question: What does the Master Theorem say about T(n) = 7*T(n/2) + n^2? (Strassen's matrix multiplication)
questions.explanation: Master Theorem: a=7, b=2, f(n)=n^2. n^(log_2 7) ≈ n^2.807. Compare: n^2.807 > n^2, so case 1: T(n) = O(n^(log_2 7)) ≈ O(n^2.807). Strassen reduces 8 multiplications to 7, saving one recursive call and breaking O(n^3).

questions.question: What does the Master Theorem say about T(n) = 2*T(n/4) + sqrt(n)?
questions.explanation: Master Theorem: a=2, b=4, f(n)=sqrt(n)=n^0.5. n^(log_4 2)=n^0.5. f(n)=n^0.5 = Theta(n^(log_b a)), so case 2: T(n) = O(n^0.5 * log n) = O(sqrt(n) log n).

questions.question: For the recurrence T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + n*log(n), which case of Master Theorem applies?
options: The standard Master Theorem does not directly apply
questions.explanation: a=2, b=2, f(n)=n log n. n^(log_2 2)=n. f(n)=n log n. For case 2, f must be Theta(n^c * log^k n) with k >= 0. Here f(n) = n*log(n) = n^1 * log^1(n), so k=1 ≥ 0 — this is actually an extended case 2: T(n) = O(n log^2 n). This is the recurrence for HeapSort-like algorithms.

questions.question: Can the Master Theorem be applied to T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1)?
options: No, the Master Theorem requires subproblems to be fractions of n (T(n/b))
questions.explanation: The Master Theorem applies to recurrences of the form T(n) = a*T(n/b) + f(n). T(n-1) decreases by a constant, not by a factor. For such recurrences, the iteration/substitution method is used instead: T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 = T(n-2) + 2 = ... = O(n).

At any point during execution, the call stack holds one frame per active recursive call. The deepest recursion occurs at factorial(0), with the chain factorial(n)→factorial(n-1)→...→factorial(0): n+1 frames simultaneously on the stack. Space = O(n).

At any point, only one branch is active (binary search never has two simultaneous active calls). The maximum call stack depth equals the number of halvings: log2(n). Space = O(log n). An iterative version achieves O(1) space.

questions.question:
What is the space complexity of recursive merge sort?

# Uses auxiliary arrays in merge
# Recursion depth is O(log n)
questions.explanation: Merge sort requires O(n) auxiliary space for the merge step. At each level of recursion, the merge operations collectively use O(n) temporary space. The recursion depth is O(log n), so the call stack uses O(log n) space. Dominant term: O(n) for the auxiliary arrays.

Despite O(2^n) total calls (time), the space (maximum simultaneous call stack depth) is only O(n). At any moment, only the deepest current branch is on the stack. The maximum depth occurs along the leftmost path: fib(n)→fib(n-1)→...→fib(0), depth n+1.

questions.question:
What is the space complexity of the Towers of Hanoi?

def hanoi(n, src, tgt, aux):
    if n == 0: return
    hanoi(n-1, src, aux, tgt)
    print(...)
    hanoi(n-1, aux, tgt, src)
questions.explanation: Like Fibonacci, the time complexity is O(2^n) but the space (call stack depth) is O(n). The deepest the stack ever gets is n (along the leftmost path hanoi(n)→hanoi(n-1)→...→hanoi(0)). Each frame uses O(1). Space = O(n).

questions.question:
What is the space complexity of DFS on a tree with n nodes and height h?

def dfs(node):
    if node is None: return
    visit(node)
    dfs(node.left)
    dfs(node.right)
questions.explanation: The call stack depth equals the height of the tree, h. For a balanced tree h=O(log n); for a skewed tree h=O(n). The space complexity is O(h) not O(n) in general. Writing O(n) is technically correct as an upper bound but O(h) is more precise.

questions.question:
What is the space complexity of generating all subsets recursively?

def subsets(arr, i, current):
    if i == len(arr): print(current); return
    subsets(arr, i + 1, current)
    subsets(arr, i + 1, current + [arr[i]])
questions.explanation: The call stack depth is at most n (recursion decrements i toward n). At any moment, only one path from root to leaf is active on the stack. Each frame uses O(n) for the 'current' list copy, giving O(n^2) total stack space. However, the maximum number of simultaneous frames is O(n), so the answer O(n) refers to stack depth. Full space including list copies is O(n^2).

questions.question:
What is the space complexity of quicksort in the best case?

# Best case: pivot always splits array in half
questions.explanation: In the best case (balanced splits), the recursion tree has depth O(log n). At any moment, only one branch is active on the call stack, so the maximum stack depth is O(log n). Worst case (skewed splits): O(n) stack depth.

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of memoized Fibonacci?

def fib(n, memo={}):
    if n in memo: return memo[n]
    if n <= 1: return n
    memo[n] = fib(n-1, memo) + fib(n-2, memo)
    return memo[n]
questions.explanation: With memoization, each subproblem fib(k) for k=0..n is computed exactly once. After the first computation, subsequent lookups are O(1). Total unique subproblems: n+1. Each is computed in O(1) after subproblems are available. Time = O(n). Space also improves from O(2^n) calls to O(n) distinct states.

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of memoized grid path counting?

def paths(m, n, memo={}):
    if (m, n) in memo: return memo[(m, n)]
    if m == 1 or n == 1: return 1
    memo[(m, n)] = paths(m-1, n, memo) + paths(m, n-1, memo)
    return memo[(m, n)]
questions.explanation: With memoization, each unique (m, n) pair is computed at most once. There are m*n unique subproblems (m values 1..m, n values 1..n). Each is computed in O(1) once its sub-results are available. Total time = O(m*n), down from O(2^(m+n)) without memoization.

options: Yes, tail recursion reduces time from O(n) to O(log n)
No, time complexity stays O(n); tail recursion only potentially reduces space complexity
Yes, tail recursion eliminates all recursion, making it O(1)
No, tail recursion increases time due to extra parameter passing
questions.explanation: Tail recursion does not change time complexity — the function still makes n recursive calls, each doing O(1) work: O(n) total. The benefit is space: a tail-call-optimizing compiler/interpreter can reuse the same stack frame, reducing space from O(n) to O(1). Python does not perform TCO, so space remains O(n) in Python.

questions.question:
What is the time complexity improvement when replacing naive Fibonacci with bottom-up DP?

# Naive: O(2^n)
# DP builds fib[0..n] iteratively
options: From O(2^n) to O(n log n)
No improvement — DP and recursion have the same complexity
questions.explanation: Bottom-up DP computes each fib[k] exactly once in O(1) using previously stored values. Total: O(n) time and O(n) space (or O(1) space if only the last two values are kept). This is a dramatic improvement from the O(2^n) exponential recursion due to eliminating redundant recomputation.

Recurrence: T(n) = 4*T(n/2) + O(1). Master Theorem: a=4, b=2, f(n)=1. n^(log_2 4)=n^2. Since n^2 >> O(1), case 1: T(n) = O(n^2)... wait: recheck. n^(log_2 4) = n^2 and f(n) = 1, so case 1 gives T(n) = O(n^2). Correction: this is O(n^2), not O(n). Each level has 4^k nodes at depth k, processing n/2^k elements. Sum = O(n^2).

This linearly scans an n×n matrix element by element. Total cells = n^2. Each call processes one cell and either returns or makes one recursive call. Total recursive calls = n^2 in the worst case. Recurrence: T(n^2) = T(n^2 - 1) + O(1) → T(n) = O(n^2) for n×n input.

Kadane's algorithm implemented recursively. Each call processes one element and makes one recursive call with n-1. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) → T(n) = O(n). The max() calls are O(1). This is a linear scan disguised as recursion.

Worst case: array is sorted, requiring comparison of all n-1 adjacent pairs. Each call does O(1) and recurses with i+1. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1) → O(n). Best case: O(1) if first two elements are out of order.

When exp is even: T(exp) = T(exp/2) + O(1) — halves the problem. When exp is odd: T(exp) = T(exp-1) + O(1), then the next call is even and halves. The problem at most doubles the steps: T(exp) = O(log exp). This is modular fast exponentiation used in cryptography.

Each element is visited once (O(n) visits). However, the list concatenation result += flatten(item) copies the result list at each level. In the worst case (deeply nested with d levels), an element at depth d is copied d times during the unwinding. Total work = O(n * d). Using .extend() instead of += reduces this by a constant but not asymptotically.

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of this function?

def merge_k_sorted(arrays, lo, hi):
    # arrays is a list of k sorted arrays, total n elements
    if lo == hi:
        return arrays[lo]
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    left = merge_k_sorted(arrays, lo, mid)
    right = merge_k_sorted(arrays, mid + 1, hi)
    return merge(left, right)  # O(n) for n total elements
questions.explanation: This is a divide-and-conquer merge of k sorted arrays with n total elements. The recursion tree has depth log2(k) (splitting k arrays). At each level, total merge work = O(n) (all elements merged once per level). Total: O(n log k). This is better than pairwise merging (O(nk)).

Recurrence: T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n). The strip check is O(n) because at most 8 points exist within each d×2d rectangle. Master Theorem case 2: T(n) = O(n log n). Note: the points must be pre-sorted by x-coordinate (O(n log n)), so total algorithm is O(n log n).

Each call right-shifts n by 1 (divides by 2). The number of bits in n is floor(log2(n)) + 1 = O(log n). Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → T(n) = O(log n) by Master Theorem case 2 (f(n)=1 = Theta(n^(log_2 1)) = Theta(1)).
Each call divides n by 2. The recursion depth equals the number of binary digits of n, which is floor(log2(n)) + 1 = O(log n). Each call does O(1) work. T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n).

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of this function?

def max_depth_tree(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0
    left_depth = max_depth_tree(root.left)
    right_depth = max_depth_tree(root.right)
    return max(left_depth, right_depth) + 1
options: O(h) where h is the height
questions.explanation: Every node must be visited to determine the maximum depth (a leaf in a deep but thin subtree determines the answer). Recurrence: T(n) = T(L) + T(R) + O(1) where L+R=n-1. Summing over all n nodes: O(n). Writing O(h) is wrong for time — O(h) is the space (stack depth), not the time to visit all nodes.

Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n). Each call does O(n) work (the loop) and recurses with n-1. Unrolling: T(n) = O(n) + O(n-1) + O(n-2) + ... + O(1) = O(n*(n+1)/2) = O(n^2). The O(n) work at each of n levels sums to O(n^2).

The two-pointer approach: each call either increments i or decrements j. Starting with i=0, j=n-1, the pointers move at most n-1 total steps before i >= j. Each call does O(1). Total calls ≤ n. T(n) = O(n). This is NOT O(n^2) — there are no nested loops, just two pointers converging.

questions.explanation: Strassen's recurrence: T(n) = 7*T(n/2) + O(n^2). Master Theorem: a=7, b=2, f(n)=n^2. n^(log_2 7) ≈ n^2.807 > n^2. Case 1: T(n) = O(n^(log_2 7)) ≈ O(n^2.807). This beats naive matrix multiplication (O(n^3)) by reducing 8 multiplications to 7.

questions.question:
What is the time complexity of this function?

def rod_cutting(price, n):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    max_val = float('-inf')
    for i in range(1, n + 1):   # O(n) loop
        max_val = max(max_val, price[i] + rod_cutting(price, n - i))
    return max_val
questions.explanation: Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + ... + T(0) + O(n). This sum satisfies T(n) = 2*T(n-1) + O(1) (each T(n-1) includes all smaller sub-calls). Without memoization: T(n) = O(2^n). Each cut decision branches into n sub-problems and overlapping subproblems are recomputed. With memoization: O(n^2).

Without memoization: T(m,n) = T(m-1,n) + T(m,n-1) + O(1). This is the same recurrence as grid path counting — exponential without memoization: O(2^(m+n)). The same cell (i,j) is recomputed exponentially many times. With memoization: O(m*n).
